Peradventure
per-ad-VEN-cher
adv.
Old French par aventure, “by chance, perhaps,” from Latin per (through, by) + adventura (a happening, a coming-to-pass). Renders the Hebrew ’ūlay, “perhaps,” and the Greek tachá and mēpote in conditional and contingent contexts.

📖 Biblical Definition

Peradventure is the KJV’s elegant archaic adverb for perhaps, by chance, if it may be—naming the contingent or uncertain. The word carries an antique register and frequently appears in moments of high pastoral or covenantal seriousness. Abraham’s great intercession for Sodom uses it across the negotiation: peradventure there be fifty righteous within the city... peradventure there shall lack five of the fifty righteous... peradventure there shall be forty found there... peradventure thirty... peradventure twenty... peradventure ten (Gen 18:24-32)—the patriarch leaning into the LORD’s mercy with the cautious uncertainty proper to a creature pleading with the Judge of all the earth. The patriarchs’ peradventures recur across Genesis: peradventure he will accept of me says Jacob of the brother he is approaching after the long years away (Gen 32:20). Solomon’s wise counsel in Proverbs uses it: contend not with a man without cause, if he have done thee no harm... lest thou learn his ways, and get a snare to thy soul—and similar prudential peradventures in the wisdom literature. The verb’s pastoral usefulness across the Bible is several. It is the proper register for the creature’s speech before the Sovereign God in matters where the outcome is hidden in His counsels (Abraham’s intercession). It is the proper register for the patriarch’s anticipation of the brother’s response in matters of relational reconciliation (Jacob’s approach to Esau). It is the proper register for the wise counsel that admits the contingencies of life’s providences (Solomon’s warnings). And it is the proper register for the apostolic and pastoral counsel that acknowledges what is hoped but cannot be presumed (Paul’s peradventure in 2 Tim 2:25, of God granting repentance to those that oppose). The KJV’s retention of peradventure over the more colorless perhaps carries the register of one who is speaking with weight, with care, with the dignity proper to matters in which God’s sovereignty and the creature’s contingency meet.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines PERADVENTURE as perhaps; it may be; by chance; in scripture, the elegant archaic adverb for what is hoped but cannot be presumed.

expand to see more

PERADVENTURE, adv. — By chance; perhaps; it may be. Peradventure there be fifty righteous within the city (Gen 18:24).

PERADVENTURE, n. — Chance; doubt; as, the conclusion is admitted without any peradventure.

📖 Key Scripture

Genesis 18:24 — "Peradventure there be fifty righteous within the city: wilt thou also destroy and not spare the place for the fifty righteous that are therein?"

Genesis 32:20 — "And say ye moreover, Behold, thy servant Jacob is behind us. For he said, I will appease him with the present that goeth before me, and afterward I will see his face; peradventure he will accept of me."

2 Timothy 2:25 — "In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth."

Romans 5:7 — "For scarcely for a righteous man will one die: yet peradventure for a good man some would even dare to die."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Peradventure is corrupted (by the standards of modern accessibility) by being replaced with the colorless perhaps—losing the register of weighty conditional speech that suits Abraham’s intercession, Jacob’s approach to Esau, Paul’s instruction to those that oppose, and the wisdom literature’s prudential counsel.

expand to see more

Modern translations uniformly replace peradventure with perhaps or it may be. The substitution is grammatically defensible; the loss is rhetorical. Peradventure carries a register of weight, dignity, and the acknowledgment of contingency that perhaps in modern usage has not retained. Abraham’s intercession for Sodom, with its six-fold peradventure, is a sustained piece of cautious pleading before the Judge of all the earth—the verb in the patriarch’s mouth is doing rhetorical work in setting the tone of his negotiation with the LORD. Replace each peradventure with perhaps, and the rhetorical weight thins; replace each with maybe, and the patriarch begins to sound like a man chatting about weekend plans. The KJV’s antique register is here doing pastoral and rhetorical work the modernizations cannot replicate.

The recovery of the KJV vocabulary is therefore not antiquarianism. It is the recovery of a register of speech the modernizations have lost, in a Bible that uniquely shaped the English Christian piety of four centuries. Modern translations have their proper uses (the new convert, the reader unable to parse the older idiom, the comparative cross-check); but the saint who learns to read the KJV in its own register hears Scripture in a vocabulary register the modernization has, sometimes, quietly flattened. Peradventure is a small specimen of the larger pattern: a word that does work the colorless substitute cannot do, retained in the KJV, available to the saint who will learn its register. The case for retaining it is the same case for retaining the King James Bible itself: not the rejection of modernization but the recognition that the older language is, in many of its places, doing things the modernizations cannot reproduce.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old French par aventure (by chance) from Latin per + adventura; renders Hebrew ’ūlay (perhaps) and Greek tachá, mēpote in conditional contexts—the elegant archaic adverb for what is hoped but cannot be presumed.

expand to see more

Hebrew ’ūlay (H194) — perhaps, peradventure (Gen 18:24-32; Josh 14:12; 1 Sam 14:6; 1 Kgs 18:5; Jonah 1:6).

Greek tachá (G5029) — perhaps, peradventure (Rom 5:7; Phlm 15).

Greek mēpote (G3379) — lest perhaps, if perhaps (2 Tim 2:25).

Old French par aventure — by chance (the etymological source).

Usage

"Peradventure there be fifty righteous within the city—Abraham’s six-fold intercession for Sodom is sustained by the verb’s cautious-pleading register."

"Peradventure is the proper register for matters where the outcome is hidden in God’s sovereign counsels and the creature speaks with weight and care."

"Modern perhaps flattens the rhetorical work the KJV’s peradventure performs; the older word carries weight the substitute has lost."
